brief: A workbench organizer: two storeys, bins on top, a drawer below, all edges capped.

requirements.evidence: A compact unit with drawer and bin storage. It is staged with a marker and a paint brush in the bin and electrical tape in the drawer.
Ground floor: piece:0,0,0 (full) and piece:0,1,0 (half-n). Upper storey: piece:0,0,1 (full), joined by snap:0,0,0.
bin:0,0,1~hex-bin-full-div3 on the upper storey: one full-depth bin with 3 compartments. There is only one upper cell, so it is a single bin, not several.
drawer:0#0,1#cut on the cut face of the ground-floor half base, opening towards the user.
capOpenFaces added 10 solid end caps. check_build lists no open faces, and lockJoints added jointBolt:0#0,0#5.

finish.summary:
I built a two-storey workbench organiser with 25 printed parts. The ground floor is a full hex base (piece:0,0,0) with a north half base (piece:0,1,0) in front of it, on the side you work from. A drawer (drawer:0#0,1#cut) sits on the half base's cut face and opens towards you. The upper storey is a full hex base (piece:0,0,1) stacked on the rear base and snapped to it. It holds a full-depth bin with 3 compartments.

capOpenFaces put solid end caps on all 10 open edges, and lockJoints added a joint bolt so the bases can't slide apart. check_build passes with no issues and the parts don't collide.

For display I put a marker and a paint brush standing in two of the bin's compartments and a roll of electrical tape in the drawer. The third compartment is empty: the configurator refused every tool I tried there because it wouldn't stay standing or hit the cell wall.

My first attempt put the drawer at the back of the build, so I undid it and re-placed the lower half base and the drawer by hand to face you. The upper storey and the bin were placed directly too.

lines.label: Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M3 x 10 socket head screw, ISO 4762
M6 x 20 socket head screw, ISO 4762
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
